name: Topical finasteride
lead: Topical finasteride is finasteride, a type II 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor, formulated for application to the scalp rather than taken as a daily tablet. It is used off-label or as a compounded or newer branded preparation for androgenetic alopecia (male and female pattern hair loss), with the stated aim of reducing the drug's systemic exposure and thereby its side effects.[1][2]

A 2018 systematic review of seven human studies reported that topical finasteride decreased the rate of hair loss and increased hair counts, with reductions in both scalp and plasma dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and no change in serum testosterone, while describing the evidence as preliminary.[3] A 2022 review with meta-analysis concluded that topical 1 percent finasteride solution was not significantly different in efficacy from oral 5 mg and 1 mg doses.[1] A phase III randomised trial of a topical finasteride spray has been published, with further phase III work in Chinese men.[4][5]

In a 2025 Delphi-based Canadian consensus, topical finasteride was among seven interventions recommended for androgenetic alopecia.[6] In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to keep finasteride's hair benefit while avoiding oral side effects; users disagree on how much it lowers serum DHT.[7][8]
infobox: Topical (solution, spray, gel; often compounded with minoxidil)
Androgenetic alopecia (male and female pattern hair loss)
Oral finasteride and topical minoxidil are the approved AGA treatments; topical finasteride is used off-label or as a regional product[3][9]

paras: Topical finasteride is used for androgenetic alopecia in men and, off-label, in women. Reviews note that only topical minoxidil and oral finasteride are approved by the FDA and EMA for the condition, and describe topical finasteride as an investigational alternative aimed at lowering systemic exposure.[3][9] Narrative reviews also discuss its use in female pattern hair loss, where oral finasteride is limited by teratogenic concern.[10] A pediatric review lists topical finasteride among options clinicians may consider for androgenetic alopecia in children and adolescents, for whom no therapy is approved.[11]

The 2018 systematic review of seven human studies found significant decreases in the rate of hair loss and increases in total and terminal hair counts, with reduced scalp and plasma DHT.[3] The 2022 meta-analysis on oral finasteride reported that finasteride 1 mg/day increased total hair count versus placebo by about 12 hairs per cm2 at 24 weeks and 16 hairs per cm2 at 48 weeks, and that efficacy of 5 mg, 1 mg and topical 1 percent solution did not differ significantly.[1]

Combination regimens with minoxidil have been tested. A 12-week randomised trial compared 0.1 percent finasteride with 5 percent minoxidil against minoxidil alone,[12] and other randomised trials examined 0.25 percent finasteride with minoxidil and a three-arm comparison with each agent alone.[13][14] An older randomised comparison of finasteride gel and tablets in 45 men also exists.[15] Reviewers generally describe the overall literature as limited by small trials, varied concentrations and short duration.[3][16]

The rationale for topical use is that oral finasteride is associated with sexual adverse events, most commonly erectile dysfunction and reduced libido, and that post-marketing reports led to a depression warning in the US label in 2011; persistent symptoms are commonly called post-finasteride syndrome.[1] The topical formulation was developed to minimise systemic exposure by acting at the follicle.[4]

The 2018 systematic review found plasma DHT fell with topical use, indicating some systemic absorption, and no change in serum testosterone.[3] A phase III spray trial specifically analysed systemic exposure relative to oral finasteride, and a phase I study characterised pharmacokinetics of a 0.25 percent spray in Chinese men.[4][17] Users in forums disagree on how much topical use reduces serum DHT (see Claims and evidence).

Finasteride inhibits type II 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme converting testosterone to DHT, which is implicated in miniaturisation of scalp follicles in androgenetic alopecia.[1] Applying it to the scalp is intended to reduce DHT locally; the studies above report measurable plasma DHT changes in some formulations.[3] Older animal work compared topical finasteride and flutamide on hamster flank organ size and enzyme activity, showing local and systemic effects.[18]

Topical finasteride appears in the consumer telehealth hair-loss market, for example in combined finasteride-minoxidil solutions that a looksmax.org member asked about when choosing between topical and oral regimens.[8] Forum users on looksmax.org and T Nation discuss it alongside topical dutasteride and other antiandrogens for people trying to avoid oral finasteride's side effects, or hair loss accompanying testosterone therapy.[7][19][20]

Human studies include a phase III randomised, placebo-controlled trial of a finasteride spray solution in men with androgenetic alopecia that also analysed systemic exposure versus oral finasteride;[4] a Chinese phase III multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled study;[5] a phase I pharmacokinetic study of 0.25 percent spray;[17] randomised trials of finasteride combined with minoxidil versus minoxidil;[12][13][14] a 45-man randomised comparison of finasteride gel with tablets;[15] and a 2018 systematic review of seven studies.[3] Several registered phase 2 and 3 trials of topical finasteride and minoxidil combinations are ongoing, completed or have unknown status.[21]

timeline.event: Hamster flank-organ study compares local and systemic effects of topical finasteride and flutamide.[18]
Randomised comparison of finasteride gel and tablets in male androgenetic alopecia published.[15]
Systematic review of seven human topical finasteride studies reports hair-count gains and reduced scalp and plasma DHT.[3]
Phase III randomised trial of topical finasteride spray published.[4]
Canadian Delphi consensus recommends topical finasteride among seven interventions for androgenetic alopecia.[6]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and T Nation, topical finasteride is discussed as a compromise for men who want to treat hair loss but fear oral finasteride side effects, and users also trade home-mixed variants and report disagreement about whether it spares serum DHT.[7][8][20]

claims.claim: Topical finasteride only lowers scalp DHT, so it avoids oral side effects
claims.believers: Posters on T Nation explain that the topical route 'stops the conversion only in the areas applied', and a looksmax.org member asks whether topical use would 'not nuke my systemic DHT' as much as a pill.[8][23]
claims.experts: A 2018 systematic review reported that both scalp and plasma DHT decreased with topical finasteride, with no change in serum testosterone, and called results preliminary.[3] A phase III trial was designed to compare systemic exposure with oral finasteride.[4]

claims.claim: Topical finasteride lowers serum DHT about as much as the oral drug
claims.believers: A T Nation poster states that topical finasteride 'appears to lower serum DHT in a magnitude similar to oral finasteride' and that it enters the bloodstream.[20]
claims.experts: The 2018 review found plasma DHT fell with topical use, indicating systemic absorption, while reviewers describe trials of fixed concentrations that vary in design.[3][16]

claims.claim: A slowly escalating ultra-low topical dose lets the body adjust and lowers side-effect risk
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user describes stepping up through increasing concentrations mixed into minoxidil solution and reports no side effects, while labelling it his own theory with 'no real scientific backing'.[7]
claims.experts: No published trial has tested gradual dose escalation of topical finasteride as a way to reduce adverse effects.

claims.claim: Topical dutasteride or other antiandrogens avoid the serum DHT effect of topical finasteride
claims.believers: A T Nation user reports controlling hair loss with topical dutasteride, mesotherapy and other agents and says topical dutasteride 'does not reduce serum DHT, just scalp DHT'.[19]
claims.experts: The sources reviewed on topical finasteride do not evaluate topical dutasteride; a review of androgenetic alopecia therapies notes dutasteride has produced better responses than finasteride in some work, mostly for the oral route.[22]

card.summary: Scalp-applied finasteride aimed at cutting systemic DHT and side effects; trial data are encouraging but smaller than for the oral drug.
card.aka: Finasteride spray / solution / gel; compounded finasteride-minoxidil
card.note: Reviews describe real but variable systemic DHT reduction; the oral drug carries documented sexual and mood adverse-event reports.

quick.overview:
Topical finasteride puts the hair-loss drug finasteride on the scalp as a spray, solution or gel instead of a daily pill, often mixed with minoxidil. The goal is to keep hair benefits while reducing whole-body exposure.

Small randomised trials, a phase III spray trial and a systematic review report hair-count gains, and one meta-analysis found no significant efficacy difference from oral finasteride. Evidence is smaller and less standardised than for the oral drug.
quick.mechanism: Finasteride blocks type II 5-alpha-reductase, which converts testosterone to DHT, a hormone linked to scalp follicle miniaturisation. Applied topically, it lowers scalp DHT; studies also report some drop in plasma DHT.
quick.risks: Oral finasteride is associated with sexual side effects and a depression warning in the US label, and persistent symptoms are discussed as post-finasteride syndrome. Topical use was designed to reduce systemic exposure but still lowers plasma DHT in studies. It is prescription-only or off-label in most settings, and concentrations and formulations vary.
